notes.meaning: Jesus promises that some of the people standing with Him will not die before seeing the kingdom of God arrive with power. Most teachers see this promise fulfilled just days later in the transfiguration, which gave the disciples a preview of Christ's royal majesty. Others understand it as pointing to His resurrection or the arrival of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.

differ.view: Some teach that Jesus was referring to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 as a visible demonstration of His royal judgment.
Some hold that Jesus meant certain listeners would live to see the beginning of the final judgment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars debate whether the saying refers to the transfiguration, the resurrection, Pentecost, or the second coming, though many favor the transfiguration because of where Mark places the verse.

notes.meaning: Six days later, Jesus leads Peter, James, and John up a high mountain away from the crowds. While there, His appearance completely changes before them, allowing His divine glory to shine out. He chose these three disciples to serve as special witnesses of His true greatness.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: The Orthodox Church teaches that the light on the mountain was the uncreated glory of God's own nature, revealed not by changing Christ, but by opening the disciples' eyes to see Him as He truly is.

notes.meaning: Jesus' clothing becomes brilliantly white, far brighter than any bleacher on earth could ever make it. The shining light did not come from an outside lamp, but poured out from Jesus Himself. This radiant purity gave the disciples a breathtaking picture of heaven.

Moses and Elijah appear on the mountain and begin talking with Jesus. Moses represents the Law, and Elijah represents the Prophets. Their presence shows that all the Old Testament Scriptures point to Jesus and find their true purpose in Him.

Peter speaks up and tells Jesus how good it is for them to be there. He offers to build three shelters out of branches, one each for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah. In his excitement, Peter makes the mistake of putting Moses and Elijah on the exact same level as Jesus.

Peter makes this awkward suggestion because he and the other two disciples are terrified. The awesome sight of heavenly glory leaves them overwhelmed with fear. Peter simply blurts out words because he does not know what else to say.

A bright cloud covers them, reminding the disciples of the cloud of God's presence that led Israel in the wilderness. The voice of God the Father speaks from the cloud, naming Jesus as His dearly loved Son. The Father commands them to listen to Jesus above every other teacher, including Moses and Elijah.

When the disciples look around, the cloud and the two ancient prophets have vanished. Only Jesus remains with them on the mountainside. This makes it clear that Jesus stands alone as the supreme Savior who stays with His followers even after special visions fade.

As they walk back down the mountain, Jesus firmly orders the three disciples not to tell anyone what they saw until He rises from the dead. Before His death, the public would misunderstand His glory and expect a political ruler. After the resurrection, the true purpose of His suffering and glory could be proclaimed clearly.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: The Orthodox Church teaches that the disciples were shown Christ's risen glory in advance so that their faith would not collapse when they saw Him suffer on the cross.

notes.meaning: The disciples obey Jesus and keep the vision completely to themselves. Still, they quietly debate among themselves what He meant by rising from the dead. They believed in the general resurrection at the end of time, but they could not understand how the Messiah Himself would die and rise soon.

The disciples ask Jesus why the teachers of the law claim that Elijah must come back first. This expectation came from the prophet Malachi, who foretold that Elijah would prepare the way for the Lord. Having just seen Elijah on the mountain, the disciples wonder how that prophecy fits with Jesus' talk about dying.

Jesus confirms that Elijah must indeed come first to prepare the people and restore things. Yet He points the disciples back to what the Scriptures teach about the Messiah. The Old Testament foretold that the Son of Man must suffer terrible pain and be completely rejected by men.

Jesus explains that the promised Elijah has already arrived in the person of John the Baptist. The rulers treated John cruelly and put him to death, exactly as the prophets suggested would happen to God's messenger. In the very same way, the religious leaders would soon mistreat and reject Jesus.

When Jesus and the three disciples return to the valley, they find a large crowd surrounding the other nine disciples. Religious teachers are arguing heatedly with them. The scribes were taking advantage of Jesus' absence to criticize and embarrass His followers after they failed to heal a boy.

As soon as the crowd catches sight of Jesus, they are filled with wonder and rush forward to greet Him. His arrival was unexpected and perfectly timed to rescue His disciples from their critics. Many commentators also suggest that some lingering majesty from the mountain was still shining on His face.

Jesus steps forward and directly asks the scribes what they are arguing about with His disciples. He immediately takes control of the situation to defend His followers. The critics are caught off guard and do not answer Him.

A man in the crowd answers Jesus and explains the real reason for the dispute. He had brought his son to find Jesus, because an evil spirit had made the boy unable to speak. Since Jesus was up on the mountain, the father had turned to the nine disciples for help.

The father describes how the evil spirit violently attacks his son, slamming him to the ground, causing him to foam at the mouth, grind his teeth, and waste away. The father had begged the disciples to drive the demon out, but they were unable to do it. Their public failure left the father crushed and the disciples humiliated.

Jesus sighs with sorrow at the persistent lack of faith, asking how long He must put up with such stubborn unbelief. His words touch the crowd, the arguing scribes, the father, and the failing disciples alike. Yet He shows His deep mercy by commanding them to bring the suffering boy straight to Him.

When the boy is brought forward and the evil spirit sees Jesus, the demon immediately throws the child into a violent seizure. The boy falls to the ground and rolls around, foaming at the mouth. Knowing its time is nearly up, the demon makes one last desperate effort to torment the child before Jesus acts.

Jesus calmly asks the father how long the child has suffered like this, and the father answers that it started in early childhood. Jesus asks this so everyone can see how chronic and severe the boy's condition really is. The answer also shows that this awful misery was not caused by any personal sin the child had committed.

The father explains that the evil spirit has repeatedly thrown the boy into fires and water to kill him. Heartbroken by years of struggle and the disciples' failure, the father pleads for help if Jesus is able to do anything. His request shows deep love for his son, even though his faith has been badly shaken.

Jesus repeats the father's words back to him, showing that the real issue is not whether Jesus has power, but whether the father has faith. God's mighty power is limitless for anyone who puts their trust in Him. Our own lack of faith is often what closes the door to the help God wants to give.

The father immediately cries out in tears, saying that he does believe, but begging Jesus to help his lingering unbelief. He honestly admits the struggle inside his heart without trying to pretend he has strong faith. Jesus welcomes this humble cry and never turns away someone who brings their doubts honestly to Him.

Seeing a curious crowd running over, Jesus moves quickly to rebuke the unclean spirit. He directly commands the deaf and mute spirit to leave the boy and never return. By commanding it never to enter again, Jesus gives the father total assurance that his son is healed for good.
